intro.title: map: change every item
intro.bodyMarkdown:
You have written loops that build a new array by changing each item: double every number, get each user's name. That job is so common that arrays have a method for it, **`map`**.

```
const prices = [4, 10, 2.5]
const doubled = prices.map((p) => p * 2)
console.log(doubled)
```

`map` calls your function once for each item, and puts what it returns into a **new** array of the same length, in the same order. The original array is left alone.

The function gets the item, and also its index if you ask for a second parameter:

```
const names = ["Ana", "Ben", "Cal"]
console.log(names.map((name) => name.toUpperCase()))
console.log(names.map((name, i) => `${i + 1}. ${name}`))
```

`map` is perfect for pulling one property out of a list of objects, or for turning each object into a new shape:

```
const users = [
  { name: "Ana", age: 31 },
  { name: "Ben", age: 25 },
]
console.log(users.map((u) => u.name))
console.log(users.map((u) => ({ ...u, adult: u.age >= 18 })))
```

Two habits to keep: always `return` a value from the callback (with `{ }` you need the word `return`), and use `map` only when you want the new array. To just *do* something for each item, like logging, use `forEach` or `for…of`.

intro.title: filter: keep what matches
intro.bodyMarkdown:
The other everyday loop keeps only some items: the adults, the cheap ones, the words that start with "a". That is **`filter`**.

```
const ages = [12, 31, 17, 45, 8]
const adults = ages.filter((age) => age >= 18)
console.log(adults)
```

Your callback is a **test**: it returns `true` to keep the item and `false` to drop it. `filter` gives back a new array of the items that passed, in their original order. It can be shorter than the original, or even empty.

Tests can be as detailed as you need, and work well on arrays of objects:

```
const books = [
  { title: "Dune", pages: 412, read: true },
  { title: "Emma", pages: 474, read: false },
  { title: "Holes", pages: 233, read: false },
]
console.log(books.filter((b) => !b.read))
console.log(books.filter((b) => !b.read && b.pages < 300))
```

The callback can return anything truthy or falsy, so `words.filter((w) => w)` keeps the non-empty strings. Clearer code says what it means, though: `words.filter((w) => w !== "")`.

A handy trick: filtering with the index removes duplicates, keeping each item only where it first appears: `list.filter((x, i) => list.indexOf(x) === i)`. (A `Set` does the same: `[...new Set(list)]`.)

To remove an item without changing the original array, filter it out: `todo.filter((t) => t !== "dishes")`.

intro.title: find: the first match
intro.bodyMarkdown:
`filter` gives every match. Often you want just one: the user with this id, the first score over 90. **`find`** returns the first item that passes your test, and stops looking as soon as it finds it.

```
const users = [
  { id: 1, name: "Ana" },
  { id: 2, name: "Ben" },
  { id: 3, name: "Cal" },
]
console.log(users.find((u) => u.id === 2))
console.log(users.find((u) => u.id === 9))
```

When nothing matches, `find` gives `undefined`, so check before using the result: `user ? user.name : "Unknown"`, or the shortcut `user?.name ?? "Unknown"` (`?.` gives `undefined` instead of an error when `user` is missing).

**`findIndex`** returns the *position* of the first match instead, or `-1` if there is none. It is what you need to change or remove an item in place.

```
const scores = [55, 72, 91, 98]
console.log(scores.findIndex((s) => s > 90))
console.log(scores.findIndex((s) => s > 100))
```

`findLast` and `findLastIndex` do the same from the end, giving the *last* match.

For a plain value, the simpler tools you already know still fit: `includes(x)` for yes or no, and `indexOf(x)` for its position. Use `find` when the test is more than "equals this", or the items are objects.

intro.title: some and every: yes-or-no questions
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Sometimes you don't need the matching items, just an answer: *is there* a late payment? *Are all* the boxes ticked? **`some`** and **`every`** answer with `true` or `false`.

```
const scores = [72, 41, 88, 95]
console.log(scores.some((s) => s < 50))
console.log(scores.every((s) => s >= 50))
```

`some` is `true` if **at least one** item passes the test. `every` is `true` only if **all** of them do. Both stop early: `some` at the first pass, `every` at the first fail.

They are the list versions of `||` and `&&`, and read almost like English:

```
const tasks = [
  { title: "plan", done: true },
  { title: "build", done: false },
]
const allDone = tasks.every((t) => t.done)
const started = tasks.some((t) => t.done)
console.log(allDone, started)
```

intro.title: reduce: boil a list down to one value
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Totals, counts and "the biggest" all walk a list carrying one running value along. **`reduce`** does exactly that.

```
const prices = [4, 10, 2.5]
const total = prices.reduce((sum, p) => sum + p, 0)
console.log(total)
```

`reduce` takes two things: a callback and a **starting value** (`0` here). The callback gets the running value so far (often called the *accumulator*, here `sum`) and the current item, and returns the new running value. After the last item, that value is the answer.

For `[4, 10, 2.5]` it goes: start at `0`; `0 + 4` is `4`; `4 + 10` is `14`; `14 + 2.5` is `16.5`.

The running value can be anything: a number, text, an array or an object. Here it is the biggest so far, then an object of counts:

```
const scores = [72, 95, 41]
console.log(scores.reduce((best, s) => Math.max(best, s), -Infinity))

const votes = ["cat", "dog", "cat"]
const counts = votes.reduce((acc, v) => {
  acc[v] = (acc[v] ?? 0) + 1
  return acc
}, {})
console.log(counts)
```

Always give the starting value. Without it, `reduce` uses the first item as the start, which breaks on an empty list (an error) and on lists of objects.

`reduce` can do almost anything, but that doesn't mean it should: `map`, `filter` or a plain loop are often clearer. It shines for sums, counts and building one object from a list.

intro.title: Sorting
intro.bodyMarkdown:
**`sort`** puts an array in order. With no argument it sorts items **as text**, which is fine for words but a trap for numbers:

```
console.log(["pear", "apple", "fig"].sort())
console.log([10, 9, 100, 1].sort())
```

`"100"` comes before `"9"` as text, just as "b" comes before "c". To sort numbers, give `sort` a **compare function**. It gets two items, `a` and `b`, and returns a negative number if `a` goes first, positive if `b` goes first, and 0 if they tie. For numbers, `a - b` does exactly that:

```
const nums = [10, 9, 100, 1]
console.log([...nums].sort((a, b) => a - b))
console.log([...nums].sort((a, b) => b - a))
```

`a - b` is smallest first; `b - a` is biggest first. For objects, compare a property: `people.sort((a, b) => a.age - b.age)`. For text, use `a.localeCompare(b)`, which also handles capitals and accents sensibly.

Careful: `sort` changes the array itself (and returns it). To keep the original, copy first with `[...list].sort(…)`, or use **`toSorted`**, which gives back a sorted copy.

```
const scores = [72, 95, 41]
const ranked = scores.toSorted((a, b) => b - a)
console.log(ranked, scores)
```

To sort by two things, like by score and then by name for ties, compare the first and only fall back to the second when it is 0: `(a, b) => b.score - a.score || a.name.localeCompare(b.name)`. `reverse` and `toReversed` flip an array's order.

intro.title: Chaining: steps one after another
intro.bodyMarkdown:
`filter`, `map` and `toSorted` all give back a new array, so you can call the next method straight on the result. This is **chaining**, and it lets you write a whole process as a list of steps:

```
const orders = [
  { item: "tea", price: 3, paid: true },
  { item: "cake", price: 6, paid: false },
  { item: "pie", price: 5, paid: true },
]

const paidTotal = orders
  .filter((o) => o.paid)
  .map((o) => o.price)
  .reduce((sum, p) => sum + p, 0)

console.log(paidTotal)
```

Read it top to bottom: keep the paid orders, take their prices, add them up. Putting each step on its own line, starting with `.`, keeps long chains easy to read.

The order of steps matters. Filter **before** mapping when the test needs the whole object; and filter early so later steps have less to do.

A chain can end in any method: `reduce` for one value, `join` for text, `length` for a count, `slice(0, 3)` for the top few, `some` for yes or no.

```
const words = ["Sun", "moon", "Star", "comet", "Sky"]
const line = words
  .filter((w) => w[0] === w[0].toUpperCase())
  .map((w) => w.toUpperCase())
  .toSorted()
  .join(", ")
console.log(line)
```

When a chain gets long or hard to follow, give the steps names: small functions like `const isPaid = (o) => o.paid` make `orders.filter(isPaid)` read like a sentence. And if you need to see what is happening in the middle, split the chain into variables and log them.

intro.title: flat, flatMap and making lists
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Lists often hold lists: each order has items, each class has students. **`flat`** joins the inner lists into one.

```
const byDay = [["run", "read"], ["swim"], ["read", "cook"]]
console.log(byDay.flat())
```

`flat()` goes one level deep. For lists inside lists inside lists, give a depth, `flat(2)`, or `flat(Infinity)` for all the way down.

A very common pattern is "map each item to a list, then flatten". **`flatMap`** does both in one step:

```
const orders = [
  { id: 1, items: ["tea", "jam"] },
  { id: 2, items: ["bread"] },
]
console.log(orders.flatMap((o) => o.items))

const sentences = ["the cat sat", "on the mat"]
console.log(sentences.flatMap((s) => s.split(" ")))
```

`flatMap` can also *drop* items, by returning `[]`, or turn one item into several. Returning `[x]` keeps it as it is.

You also often need to **make** a list. `Array.from({ length: 5 }, (_, i) => i + 1)` builds `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]`: the function is called for each position with its index (the `_` is a name for the parameter you don't use). `Array(3).fill(0)` gives `[0, 0, 0]`. And `Array.from("hello")` splits text into letters.

```
console.log(Array.from({ length: 5 }, (_, i) => i + 1))
console.log(Array.from({ length: 4 }, (_, i) => i * i))
console.log(Array(3).fill("-"))
```

intro.title: Objects as lists: keys, values and entries
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Objects don't have `map` or `filter`. But three functions turn an object into an array, and then every list method is yours:

```
const stock = { apples: 12, pears: 0, plums: 5 }
console.log(Object.keys(stock))
console.log(Object.values(stock))
console.log(Object.entries(stock))
```

`Object.keys` gives the property names, `Object.values` the values, and `Object.entries` both, as `[key, value]` pairs. Destructuring the pairs makes loops neat:

```
const stock = { apples: 12, pears: 0, plums: 5 }
for (const [fruit, count] of Object.entries(stock)) {
  console.log(`${fruit}: ${count}`)
}
```

To go the other way, **`Object.fromEntries`** turns `[key, value]` pairs back into an object. Together they let you filter or change an object's properties:

```
const stock = { apples: 12, pears: 0, plums: 5 }
const inStock = Object.fromEntries(
  Object.entries(stock).filter(([fruit, count]) => count > 0),
)
console.log(inStock)
```

The same trick works with a `Map`: `new Map(Object.entries(obj))` and `Object.fromEntries(map)`.

Two quick ones: `Object.keys(obj).length` counts the properties, and `Object.values(obj).reduce(...)` adds up all the values.

intro.title: Grouping data
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Reports often sort things into groups: sales by month, students by class, words by first letter. **`Object.groupBy`** does it in one call. Give it a list and a function that says which group each item belongs in:

```
const pets = [
  { name: "Rex", kind: "dog" },
  { name: "Tom", kind: "cat" },
  { name: "Fido", kind: "dog" },
]
const byKind = Object.groupBy(pets, (p) => p.kind)
console.log(byKind)
```

The result is an object: each group's name is a key, and its value is the array of items in that group, in their original order. Logged, it shows as `[Object: null prototype]`: an object made without the usual built-in extras, which you use just like any other. (`Map.groupBy` does the same but gives a `Map`, which is handy when the group keys aren't text.)

The group can be anything you work out, not just a property:

```
const scores = [91, 45, 78, 62, 88]
console.log(Object.groupBy(scores, (s) => (s >= 50 ? "pass" : "fail")))
```

`groupBy` is quite new. In older code, or when you want to build something other than arrays, the same thing is done with `reduce`:

```
const words = ["apple", "avocado", "banana", "blueberry", "cherry"]
const byLetter = words.reduce((groups, w) => {
  const key = w[0]
  ;(groups[key] ??= []).push(w)
  return groups
}, {})
console.log(byLetter)
```

`groups[key] ??= []` makes the group's array the first time a key is seen (`??=` sets a value only if there isn't one yet; the `;` in front stops the line joining the one above).

After grouping, `Object.entries` turns the groups into a list to summarise: a count or total for each group.

```
const sales = [
  { month: "Jan", amount: 120 },
  { month: "Feb", amount: 80 },
  { month: "Jan", amount: 40 },
]
const groups = Object.groupBy(sales, (s) => s.month)
for (const [month, list] of Object.entries(groups)) {
  console.log(month, list.reduce((sum, s) => sum + s.amount, 0))
}
```

challenges.title: Expert: The to-watch line
challenges.promptMarkdown: Write `watchLine(movies)`, returning `To watch: Coco (8.4), Soul (8.0)`: the unwatched movies, best rated first, each rating to 1 decimal place. With nothing left, return `All watched!`.
challenges.hint: Filter, sort by `b.rating - a.rating`, map to `` `${m.title} (${m.rating.toFixed(1)})` ``, join with `", "`.
challenges.solution:
function watchLine(movies) {
  const left = movies
    .filter((m) => !m.watched)
    .toSorted((a, b) => b.rating - a.rating)
    .map((m) => `${m.title} (${m.rating.toFixed(1)})`)
  return left.length === 0 ? "All watched!" : `To watch: ${left.join(", ")}`
}
